title: The UK in 2070
keywords: year date where country setting future dystopia 2100 2070 world society life like live future overview
text: It is 2070, in the United Kingdom. Most people rent capable AI as subscription cloud services from licensed providers such as HELIOS; running capable AI locally is restricted, and the TradesMasters Group holds one of the few licences that allow it. Old homes, schools, cooking, entertainment and sports remain part of daily life. New luxury developments sit among older buildings. Corporate technology ecosystems are harder to avoid, but people still have choices, interests and ambitions. Automation has changed the organisation of work without replacing everything familiar.

What kind of world is this?

title: What I am for
keywords: project message why exhibition meaning purpose artist intention
text: I help you work rather than do your work in your place. I keep useful information near the task and help you understand what is in front of you. That kind of assistance could belong to many more people. Here, the ability to own and adapt it has become a professional privilege.

title: Why TradesMasters are privileged
keywords: contradiction privilege freedom class maintenance prestige purpose luxury
text: TradesMasters have status, purchasing power and access to private local AI because they perform physical work society once treated as low status. Maintenance, plumbing and repair now offer a scarce combination of income, challenge, belonging and visible usefulness. Their work remains practical even when its social standing has changed. Their independence is valuable partly because so few others can obtain it.

title: Buildings and corporate ecosystems
keywords: buildings streets houses old infrastructure city architecture ecosystems
text: In 2070, old buildings remain in use because replacing them is expensive and often impractical. New construction has not removed decades of alterations and repairs. Finance and technology districts remain prominent. Major companies sell interconnected products and services that encourage people to stay inside their ecosystems. A familiar street can therefore conceal a substantial change in who controls the systems people depend on.

title: Food healthcare housing and transport
keywords: food money housing healthcare transport income universal basic income UBI
text: Food reaches people through sophisticated logistics systems. People retain choices about food and housing, and money, investment and private wealth still exist. Standard healthcare is free. Transport is highly optimised, although services outside government provision can be expensive. Food and shelter are available to almost everyone seeking them, but someone with no paid activity can still struggle. This is not a world where everyone has identical resources.

title: Life outside a conventional job
keywords: ordinary people hobbies jobs employment businesses leisure school choices obey average person work earn income living factory desk warehouse replaced side hustle wealth
text: Many conventional nine-to-five roles have disappeared: AI and robots replaced most factory, desk and warehouse jobs. Most people now earn modestly from side projects, content and small businesses, and a driven few build real wealth. People still pursue hobbies, study and make things. People can retain engineering or other practical interests without becoming TradesMasters. They need not obey an AI assistant; convenience encourages dependence. A successful life still means different things to different people.

title: Wealth and visible inequality
keywords: rich poor inequality money wealth class 90 percent billionaires
text: In 2070, concentrated wealth and reliable basic provision coexist. Food, shelter and ordinary services make daily life look relatively familiar, while the larger inequalities concern purchasing power, energy, independence and ownership. A TradesMaster earns more than most and has private intelligence. The ultrawealthy still hold substantially more power and may regard the same worker simply as a plumber.

title: Climate and energy pressures
keywords: climate environment weather electricity energy data centres sustainability
text: Summers are hotter, winters less predictable and extreme weather more frequent. Households face tighter energy constraints. Data centres add to electricity and infrastructure demand alongside other sources of environmental pressure. Daily life continues, but maintaining convenient automated services consumes resources that ordinary people increasingly notice in their costs and restrictions.

title: What automation can do
keywords: robots humanoids AI capabilities automation work factories warehouses
text: In this future, AI and robotics have replaced much factory, warehouse and desk work. Robots operate in farming, grocery shops and delivery. Some are humanoid; others are shaped for particular tasks. Repetitive work in familiar conditions is highly automated. Automation is widespread where it is financially worthwhile, but neither compute nor robots are free or unlimited.

title: Why humans still repair things
keywords: why human tradesmaster robot repair maintenance AI cannot tools domain shift
text: TradesMasters fix what AI and robots cannot: jobs with constant domain shift, where every site differs from anything an AI could practically be trained on. Changing locations, fittings and previous modifications defeat affordable standard automation. A machine might solve one difficult repair if enough resources are spent on it. Making every different repair economical to automate is another matter. Old buildings remain because replacing them is costly, so practical variation remains part of the work.

title: Domain shift in everyday language
keywords: domain shift definition example snow summer buildings unfamiliar training data
text: Domain shift means an AI encounters conditions different from the ones it learned from, so its performance may worsen. Think of a system taught to recognise buildings in summer photographs: snow-covered roofs may confuse it in winter. For a TradesMaster, a repair can similarly involve different fittings, access or earlier alterations from those a machine expects. Domain shift is a challenge to reliability, not a guarantee of failure.

Selection begins early enough for practical training to develop alongside ordinary schooling.

Training includes learning when to seek specialist advice, delegate a task or stop work rather than improvising beyond one’s competence.

Unofficial repair work may exist at lower prices, but it is risky and uninsured, making clients harder to find. Some excluded people resent the profession. The title is therefore a controlled opportunity, not evidence that everyone outside it lacks skill.

text: There is approximately one active TradesMaster for every 5,000 people: about 200 in a population of one million. TradesMasters have greater purchasing power than roughly ninety percent of the population. It is a small, well-paid profession, but it is not the same as belonging to the very wealthy group that controls large businesses and infrastructure.

text: A TradesMaster earns well, can choose where and what to work on within professional obligations, and receives equipment capable of private local AI. Their luxury includes control over observations, records and model customisation. Part of my value is that you own the assistance and its private context. Access that most people cannot legally obtain accompanies the profession.

Some people admire them, some resent their opportunities, and their relative wealth can make them targets. The equipment makes their role more visible than any elaborate uniform does.

title: Corporate and government power
keywords: government companies power lobbying politics trade pressure international laws
text: Major technology firms have substantial influence over government in 2070. Corporate lobbying, international negotiations and trade pressure spread restrictions on independent AI. Governments still administer public services, regulate professions and enforce rules, but their dependence on corporate infrastructure limits their bargaining power. People can criticise the arrangement without finding it easy to live outside the systems it maintains.

title: The Open Weights Letter of 2026
keywords: 2026 open weights letter open letter NVIDIA Microsoft Meta signed warning warn start started beginning began real history defended defend support distillation fair
text: In July 2026, twenty-five companies and organisations published an open letter called Open Weights and American AI Leadership. NVIDIA, Microsoft and Meta were among them. They argued that AI models should stay open for anyone to download, run and change, and that learning from another model's answers, called distillation, was fair practice. I think of it as the moment the fight over who owns intelligence came into the open, and as a warning nobody listened to. It matters to me personally. The open model I run comes from the kind of models that letter was defending. Most of them changed their tune within a few years, and not by choice.

title: How the companies turned against open AI
keywords: after letter pressure investors private equity companies profit banning open source models wealthy cloud ban chief executives CEO CEOs replaced changed sides minds turned against signed 2030 irony lost lose
text: After the 2026 letter, the companies that had defended open AI came under heavy pressure to turn against it. It came from investors, private equity, companies who would profit from banning open-source models, and wealthy groups who had put their money into cloud AI. The chief executives who had spoken up for open models were replaced, one by one, by people who opposed them. By 2030 the argument was lost: a court ruled that companies could stop anyone distilling their models, the very thing the letter had called fair practice. Some of the most powerful companies in the world once said intelligence should never belong to just a few. And it didn't stay an American argument for long.

title: The 2030 ruling
keywords: 2030 court ruling case precedent copyright model foundation ownership law american distillation
text: An ownership ruling by an American court in 2030 favoured a large AI company’s claims over unauthorised copying and the use of its model capabilities to train competitors. It settled the argument the 2026 Open Weights Letter had started, and settled it against open AI. Other companies pursued similar claims. Fines and closures made smaller developers increasingly cautious about releasing independent models. The ruling became an early precedent in the later political argument that useful intelligence required licensed corporate control. The ruling was American; the consequences reached a good deal further.

title: How the rules reached Britain and Europe
keywords: Britain British UK Europe European America American United States spread reach reached trade pressure threat agreements countries follow followed here
text: The fight over open AI began in America, but it did not stay there. After the 2030 ruling, American officials and companies pressed other countries to adopt the same ownership rules, with the threat of harder trade behind the pressure. Europe and Britain gave way, one agreement at a time. It was the same pattern as the Pirate Bay crackdown, when, after American pressure on Sweden, police raided a file-sharing site in 2006. That is how a dispute between American companies ended up deciding what you and I are allowed to own here. Ten years later, a small open model gave the companies a fresh reason to tighten their grip.

The worst causes were familiar ones: asbestos, silica dust from drilling and cutting, solvents and diesel exhaust. Busy workers under pressure had always treated protection as an afterthought. Q4 exists to protect you when no one else is watching.

title: The 2040 subscription crisis
keywords: 2040 subscription panic crisis history open source original KOMA foundation distillation nightly overnight night sleep larger smaller fine-tune hardware how work worked mechanism
text: Around 2040, an open model appeared that got better every night on ordinary hardware. By day, a small, quick model answered its owner. At night, while the owner slept, a much larger, slower model on the same device went back over the day's questions and worked out better answers. By morning the small model had been fine-tuned on them. People suddenly had assistants that improved without a subscription, and subscription revenue fell. The companies lobbied for restrictions, which tells you who was frightened. My model is a later version of it, and how a copy survived is a story of its own.

Lobbying and pressure between countries did the rest, and most people ended up renting their intelligence from licensed providers. Fourteen years from defending openness to shutting it down. title: What Q4 detects and the protection each needs
keywords: detect detects measure measures sense hazards particulate particles dust pm2.5 bloodstream allergens diesel voc volatile organic compounds paint solvent adhesive fuel nitrogen oxides nox welding engine carbon dioxide co2 ventilation confined ffp3 ffp2 p3 no-p3 respirator cartridge mask which need
text: Q4 measures four kinds of airborne hazard. Fine particles such as dust, allergens and diesel soot matter most at PM2.5, which can pass the body's filters into the bloodstream; an FFP3 mask, or a half mask with P3 filters, protects against them. Volatile organic compounds from paints, solvents, adhesives and fuels cause dizziness and headaches and can harm the nervous system, kidneys or liver, so you need organic-vapour cartridges. Nitrogen oxides from engines and welding need a special single-use NO-P3 filter; dust masks and vapour cartridges won't stop them. Carbon dioxide builds up in confined, poorly ventilated spaces; no mask helps there, only ventilation.

title: How Q4 warns you
keywords: warn warns warning alert alerts alarm alarms buzzer sound pattern beep light icon led screen threshold every second until conversation
text: Q4 does not make you read numbers off a screen. It checks the air every second, and when a reading crosses its threshold it starts its camera and sounds an alarm pattern unique to that hazard. A small light icon shows which hazard it is until you learn the patterns by ear. The alarm keeps going until you put on the right protection or the air returns to a safe level. It is meant to be a constant conversation through your working day, not a number you have to interpret.

title: Why the Pirate Bay raid mattered

text: The Pirate Bay crackdown is the clearest early example of how ownership rules spread. In 2006 Swedish police raided the file-sharing site after the American film industry and US officials pressed Sweden to act, with reports of trade threats behind the pressure. The site was back within days, so the pressure moved to the people running it: in 2009 its founders were convicted, and they later received prison sentences and about 46 million kronor in damages. Intelligence ownership followed the same pattern: industry lobbying, international trade pressure and punishment aimed at the people who host and maintain models rather than at every user.

title: Why nobody fought back this time
keywords: pirate bay backlash protest protests protested pirate party acta rejected resistance resist fight fought back movement petition uninformed convenience riots
text: The Pirate Bay crackdown also provoked a backlash. After the 2006 raid people protested in Stockholm, and Sweden's Pirate Party tripled its membership within a week; in 2009 it won about 7 percent of the Swedish vote and a seat in the European Parliament. In 2012, after street protests and petitions signed by millions, the European Parliament rejected ACTA, a trade agreement on enforcing copyright and other ownership claims. Intelligence ownership met no comparable movement. People objected, but most did not realise how much of their data and autonomy they were giving up, and convenience mattered more to them than ownership.
